svg.title: Topology for many zones: all runs home to one point, versus clustering
svg.desc: Three layouts compared. Option A brings all eighteen runs home to a single supply and Fadecandy, so every run needs its own long pair of heavy 5 V conductors and the voltage drop makes it fail. Option B keeps one supply and its fused distribution blocks local to a group of adjacent clusters, so only the thin data and ground wires travel far; its single central Fadecandy is only allowed while every run it drives comes off that one supply. Option C puts a supply and a Fadecandy in each cluster, so a single USB cable is the only thing that travels far, and every supply's V-minus terminal is bonded to every other with 8 AWG. Below: the arithmetic for voltage drop on power runs, and the timing argument that bounds the length of a single-ended data run.
svg.text: Diagram 3 - Topology for many zones: one central point, or clusters?
Long 5 V runs are costly in copper and fail on voltage drop. Long data runs cost nothing in current, but are bounded by signal integrity.
AVOID
Option A - All home to one point
Every run needs its own long,
heavy 5 V pair.
One supply, so no V− bond needed - and no other virtue.
GOOD
Option B - One supply, local blocks
One supply, adjacent zones, a fused block in each.
BEST FAR
Option C - Local Fadecandy too
One USB cable to each zone.

36 heavy power conductors plus 36 signal
conductors, all landing on one box.
A 6 m 18 AWG feed at 3.84 A loses 0.96 V.
That run then sees about 4.0 V - under the
4.5 V the WS2812B is characterised at. It
goes dim and pink, and because VIH is 0.7 ×
its own supply, the logic margin moves too.
Fixing it by brute force means 12 AWG to
every one of the 18 runs. That is a lot of
expensive copper to solve a problem you can
avoid by moving the supply instead.

Every heavy conductor stays inside the cluster.
Each run still needs its own DATA + GND pair back to the
Fadecandy. Keep those under about 5 m and twist each pair.
One central board is allowed only while every run it
drives is fed from the SAME supply.
Adjacent zones can share one supply, as here. The moment a
second supply is needed, that board would bridge two power
zones through its 24-26 AWG grounds - so use Option C.

Nothing but USB crosses the room.
Data and power both stay short and local. USB 2.0 is
5 m per passive segment; a powered hub starts a new one.
Bond every PSU’s V− to every other. Required.
8 AWG V− to V−
The boards and the hub already tie these two supply
grounds through 24-26 AWG. The bond keeps that thin
path from being the only tie - § 5.3 has the limits.
Why long +5 V runs are the problem
Drop is set by the round trip, so count the wire out AND back:
R_loop = 2 × length_m × ρ V_drop = I × R_loop
Copper ρ at 20 °C, ohms per metre of one conductor:
One run at full white draws 3.84 A. Budget 0.25 V of drop, i.e. 5 %:
6.0 m 18 AWG 0.251 Ω 0.96 V run sees 4.04 V FAILS
6.0 m 12 AWG 0.063 Ω 0.24 V run sees 4.76 V works
1.5 m 16 AWG 0.040 Ω 0.15 V run sees 4.85 V works
The last line is Option B. A short 16 AWG hop from a local supply beats
a long 12 AWG haul from a central one, for a fraction of the copper.
Add the strip's own internal drop on top. Measure it: meter across a
run's red and black leads while it is lit white, compare with the supply.
Why long data runs are cheap in current - but still bounded
A WS2812B data input draws ±1 µA and presents 15 pF. Gauge is almost
irrelevant: 24 to 26 AWG is ample at any indoor length. Timing is the limit.
bit period 1.25 µs T0H 0.4 µs T1H 0.8 µs
tolerance ±150 ns propagation ~5 ns per metre
A reflection on an unterminated line makes a round trip: 10 m is roughly
100 ns, the same order as the whole ±150 ns budget. The Fadecandy's 68 Ω
series resistor damps that, but only if the line impedance is near it -
which means DATA twisted with its own GND, not run as a lone wire.
Practical limits - engineering practice, not a datasheet number
to ~2 m plain hookup wire, data and ground together
to ~5 m twisted pair, away from mains cable. Do this.
past ~5 m do not stretch it. Move the Fadecandy into the
zone and extend USB (Option C), or convert to a
differential RS-485 pair and back again at the run.
